Saldanha Red Dust

By: Floris Kotze | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Red dust isn’t just a nuisance in Saldanha Bay—it’s a crisis.

Unique Selling Point:
This isn’t about a few dirty walls. It’s about lives disrupted, businesses stifled, and communities fighting to breathe clean air. Iron ore dust from the port has painted the entire landscape red—houses, cars, even pets. Despite efforts by Transnet to suppress the dust, it continues to seep into every corner of the town, damaging property and peace of mind.
Imagine living in a place where opening your door means inviting a red storm into your kitchen. Where your home, no matter how many times you clean or repaint, is never truly clean. The Red Dust Action Group is trying to help, determined to hold powerful corporations accountable for polluting their community. They’re not just pushing for cleaner air—they’re pushing for justice.

Summary:
This story isn’t just local; it’s a reflection of corporate responsibility, environmental impact, and the power of a community united in action. It’s time for the world to see the red-stained truth behind Saldanha Bay.
We speak to the West Coast District Municipality (WCDM) local business, and Kumba / Transnet group, to get the facts! We discover there is a much larger crisis looming in the near future…

Travel and 1 night stay in Saldanha, Drone pilot please.

Script:


Industrial shots, harsh, ugly, we see the harsh reality of the ports, trains, dirty, harsh, then the opposite, beauty, beach - our presenter in between the shots…

Upsounds:

“People are scared to talk… because of different parties playing key roles at the West Coast.”

“In the bay we see what's happening to the fish. If we open up the mussels that we catch in the way, it's pink inside. No way. So this dust is really going everywhere.”

“Health impact over the years…. we have observed this over the years.”

We must renovate almost every few years, at the cost of around about over three million.

Interrupted by the sounds of a train.

Then presenter on beach

Link:
Saldanha Bay, a place of contrast. Beauty on the one side and then on the other, one of Africa's largest natural harbours. Perfect for exporting minerals.

VO: 1
The town lies two hours from Cape Town and has been a gateway for iron ore exports since 1976.
It has two main terminals, the iron ore terminal and the multipurpose terminal, which also handles other commodities like manganese and zinc.
All of South Africa's iron ore is exported from here.
This is TransNet's powerhouse on the west coast.
But at what cost?

Kyle:
The challenges that we face every day are enormous.
When you're living here on a long-term basis, your children come home from school, you need to wash their feet. You need to paint your house every four months. Every four months. Every four months. It's not just a Saldanha bay problem. It's a Vredenberg, a Langebaan, and a St Helena Bay problem. It's widespread across this entire region.


Driving:
“There's no question of doubt that it's killing things.”



VO: 2
Kyle Dods has every reason to be concerned about the red dust pollution in the district.
As a resident of Saldanha Bay, and acting chair of the Red Dust Action Group, he leads efforts to hold TransNet and municipalities accountable and curb the spread of red iron ore dust.
This dust originates from the TransNet port terminal, where iron ore from inland mines is loaded onto ships for export.

Kyle:
To see the emotional outpouring of people that have had their lives affected for many, many, many years, properties that are devalued, people that are unable to realise their full potential as a result of the polluted staining. It's having a dire effect on people's mental well-being within this area. And that's unacceptable. Why should any organisation be able to operate, have that kind of influence on other people's lives?

VO 3:
Driving through the area, the impact of the red dust is obvious. It clings to houses, coats the roads and even gives the plants a reddish hue.
We spoke to some of the residents and business owners to hear how it impacts their daily lives.

Carstens Voxie:
It's been here since I can remember. Obviously in the summer months, it's worse with a southeasterly wind.
Mac: Yes.
Coming straight from the iron or jetty.

VO: 4
Nicholas Carstens manages a business in Saldanha and HE SAYS the Iron ore dust has already cost the business millions in repairs and maintenance.

I mean, there's a good example on the gates. From this side, you can see it perfectly. And as you turn the gate around, it's exactly how it should be.

Mac: So it's actually the real colour. Yeah, yeah. Look at this.

Jean
Dust is there it's all around it's in the water when it rains it flows it's on the plants yeah it's a it's a it's a mess.

VO: 5
Jean Tredoux, is an Environmental Health Practitioner and is particularly concerned about the potential health effects it could have.

Jean
It's just a snowball effect for your whole business and not even mentioning people with sinus problems.

VO 6:
Kevin Maart is a community leader.


Kevin Maart Voxie:
Since Transnet's arrival our fishing has been negatively impacted and as a result, our income has declined. But there is no way Transnet will compensate us because they don't consult with the community. Since Transnet's arrival, our fishing has been negatively impacted and, as result, our income has declined.
But there is no way Transnet will compensate us because they're not interested in
consulting with the community.

VO 7:
Serious allegations from some of the residents, so we head to the TransNet terminal,
3 kilometres from town.

Oscar Borchards
So from TransNet as a corporate citizen, if you might call it, we do quarterly engagement with the community and we listen as well.

VO 8:
We spoke to Oscar Borchards, TransNet's managing executive for Western Cape terminals.

Mac
There's something that we can't ignore here. You drive around Saldanha bay Bay, you go past the houses, you go past some of the industrial park. You can see the dust and how that has impacted the community. Do you feel that the measures that are being implemented by TransNet are enough?

Oscar Borchards
Mostly of our staff comes from Saldanha.
So it is from our importance to ensure that the employees coming in, that they are obviously, that they work in a safe environment. We are measured externally in terms of how we treat the product. So we ensure that from our operational side, and our quality and our environmental, they are there to ensure that it gets treated and that we mitigate any dust.





VO 9:
The West Coast District Municipality together with Saldanha Bay Municipality form part of a multi stakeholder forum where red dust related matters are discussed. This group is also responsible for monitoring dust fallout levels to ensure Transnet stays within national limits of 600 milligrams per square metre per day - averaged over 30 days.

David Joubert
There is official visits and unofficial visits by our equality offices. And sometimes also the element of surprise.

VO 10:
David Joubert is the municipal manager for the West Coast District Municipality.

David Joubert
In terms of our legislative requirements, they are meeting that requirement. And if we are saying that that should not be the threshold, we need to have legislative reform in that regard.

VO 11:
It’s not as straightforward as it seems. Amending regulations requires trusted, reliable data. While Transnet’s dust fallout levels may be below national standards, the accuracy of some measurement methods is, shall we say, questionable...

Link:
This bucket system is supposed to be collecting all dust particles, but it's really inefficient with all of this wind. The dust goes above, it goes below, it hits against the bucket, so you don't really get a proper measure of how much dust is actually collected.

VO 12:
The bucket monitoring system, used by both the municipality and Transnet, is widely deployed but largely ineffective. It relies on low wind speeds and close placement to dust sources for accuracy. Vandalism frequently disrupts data collection, and the 30-day sampling period further delays detection, with exceedances identified weeks too late.

Kyle:
If you have a huge stream of dust that occurs and completely blankets out an enormous ship. How do you expect that dust to drift two to three kilometres away and fall within that bucket in order for you to take that bucket and measure it and go, oh, you are well within the limits? And not only that, but they have decide - the fact that it has an average fallout over a 30-day period. So in other words, they may have a massive spike of dust, which is going to pollute this entire environment. Yet because it's averaged out of a 30-day period, it falls within the limitations.




Carmen
Last year, December 2023, I took a video of the iron ore (dust) floating on the water. Nowhere do they mention whether iron ore is being detected in water samples.

VO 13:
Carmen Rogers is an activist and traditional leader from Langebaan, a town neighbouring Saldanha Bay.

Carmen
Some people complain a lot about their chest, like asthma.
I am using a nebuliser. That is how dire the situation is.

VO 14:
Proving a direct link between health issues and iron ore dust exposure in the area, requires long-term research and has not yet been established. However, a recent University of Cape Town survey of 241 people in the area, has highlighted some of the community's concerns.

Dr. Itumeleng Ntatamala
A high proportion of the participants indicating that they believed that they had health problems caused by exposure to the minedust.

Dr. Itumeleng Ntatamala, an Occupational Medicine Specialist and Senior Lecturer at the University of Cape Town, played a crucial role in conducting and interpreting the survey’s results.

Dr. Itumeleng Ntatamala
There is evidence that inhalation of mineral dust both in workplaces and in the general population does result in adverse health outcomes. It can be respiratory health outcomes, neurological skin problems, etc.
What the study does show, however, is that community members do have ailments that they have reported, including worsening of asthma and other respiratory conditions, which they they blame the air pollution and the Minedust for.

Upsound Kevin
People who used to work at the terminal developed lung infections, even lung cancer. We have a lot of lung cancer cases. What really angers me is that Transnet is ignoring our fishing community in the process.






Kyle
In general cases, it points to the fact that iron ore does not have a negative impact on human health. But when you look at the responses overwhelmingly, they point to the fact that they have negative health consequences as a result of moving into this area. So the sentiment on one side is very different to what the so-called facts are pointing out.

David Joubert
We have not received any confirmation or information that the red dust has created a health issue in the community. If that is the case, we have in the past requested those complainers to provide us with a scientifically or a specialist report reflecting that it's actually because of the dust.

Mac
Should we perhaps not be going above and beyond so that the community isn't as impacted?

Oscar Borchards
We have regular engagement with the community. There is a complaints register that we are recording. And secondly, we engage for particular things. If there's anything coming up, we will then go back in terms of that one.

VO 15:
A dedicated group specialising in air quality, is working to influence legislation changes, but the process is complex, requiring public participation, input from provincial and national forums, and solid scientific evidence to address widespread issues effectively.

Kyle
It's not up to legislation to force that change. It's down to the operators to go, what we're doing is not good enough. What we need to do is stand up and do better. Why wouldn't you as an organisation want to see this entire era flourishing?

Link
I mean, look at this, turquoise water, it's really, really quiet. I mean, I can see myself sitting somewhere here, sipping on a cocktail and watching the sunset.
But when you think of that Red Dust that just covers everything and just puts a blanket over such beauty, I would also be upset.


Carmen Rodgers Upsound
It is not about race, colour or religion. It affects all of us. We can't allow them [Transnet] to continue to handle the iron ore in such an unsafe manner.
They have to implement more measures to ensure our safety.



PROMO ONE

VO: Saldanha Bay is facing an unusual crisis

UPSOUND:

VO: A layer of thick red dust envelopes the city and residents are powerless to stop it.

UPSOUND:



PROMO TWO

VO: In Saldanha Bay, iron ore from the harbour, has become an unbearable stain on the community.

UPSOUND:

VO: Homes, vehicles, and even pets haven’t been spared from the thick layer of red dust that envelopes the city.


PROMO Three

VO: Lives disrupted… businesses stifled, and a community fighting to breathe clean air again.

UPSOUND:

VO: As a thick layer of red dust envelopes the city, residents have had enough.

It can be respiratory health outcomes, neurological skin problems, etc. What the study does show, however, is that community members do have ailments that they have reported, including worsening of asthma and other respiratory conditions, which they they blame the air pollution and the Minedust for. Upsound Kevin People who used to work at the terminal developed lung infections, even lung cancer. We have a lot of lung cancer cases. What really angers me is that Transnet is ignoring our fishing community in the process. Kyle In general cases, it points to the fact that iron ore does not have a negative impact on human health. But when you look at the responses overwhelmingly, they point to the fact that they have negative health consequences as a result of moving into this area. So the sentiment on one side is very different to what the so-called facts are pointing out. David Joubert We have not received any confirmation or information that the red dust has created a health issue in the community. If that is the case, we have in the past requested those complainers to provide us with a scientifically or a specialist report reflecting that it's actually because of the dust. Mac Should we perhaps not be going above and beyond so that the community isn't as impacted? Oscar Borchards We have regular engagement with the community. There is a complaints register that we are recording. And secondly, we engage for particular things. If there's anything coming up, we will then go back in terms of that one. VO 15: A dedicated group specialising in air quality, is working to influence legislation changes, but the process is complex, requiring public participation, input from provincial and national forums, and solid scientific evidence to address widespread issues effectively. Kyle It's not up to legislation to force that change. It's down to the operators to go, what we're doing is not good enough. What we need to do is stand up and do better. Why wouldn't you as an organisation want to see this entire era flourishing? Link I mean, look at this, turquoise water, it's really, really quiet. I mean, I can see myself sitting somewhere here, sipping on a cocktail and watching the sunset. But when you think of that Red Dust that just covers everything and just puts a blanket over such beauty, I would also be upset. Carmen Rodgers Upsound It is not about race, colour or religion. It affects all of us. We can't allow them [Transnet] to continue to handle the iron ore in such an unsafe manner. They have to implement more measures to ensure our safety. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Red dust isn’t just a nuisance in Saldanha Bay—it’s a crisis.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: This isn’t about a few dirty walls. It’s about lives disrupted, businesses stifled, and communities fighting to breathe clean air. Iron ore dust from the port has painted the entire landscape red—houses, cars, even pets. Despite efforts by Transnet to suppress the dust, it continues to seep into every corner of the town, damaging property and peace of mind. Imagine living in a place where opening your door means inviting a red storm into your kitchen. Where your home, no matter how many times you clean or repaint, is never truly clean. The Red Dust Action Group is trying to help, determined to hold powerful corporations accountable for polluting their community. They’re not just pushing for cleaner air—they’re pushing for justice.
metadata.Summary: This story isn’t just local; it’s a reflection of corporate responsibility, environmental impact, and the power of a community united in action. It’s time for the world to see the red-stained truth behind Saldanha Bay. We speak to the West Coast District Municipality (WCDM) local business, and Kumba / Transnet group, to get the facts! We discover there is a much larger crisis looming in the near future…
